claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1A,C and E

claims.claim: At 6 months of age, about 75 M1 ipRGCs survived in Opn4LacZ/DTA mice.
claims.source: Using the LacZ locus with the aDTA or DTA loci, we show that at 6 months of age, about 75 M1 ipRGCs survived in Opn4LacZ/DTA mice (Supplementary file 1), and consistent with our previous report, about 125 M1 ipRGCs survived in Opn4LacZ/aDTA mice (Güler et al., 2008) (Figure 1F; Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1F and Supplementary file 1

claims.claim: About 125 M1 ipRGCs survived in Opn4LacZ/aDTA mice at 6 months of age.
claims.source: Using the LacZ locus with the aDTA or DTA loci, we show that at 6 months of age, about 75 M1 ipRGCs survived in Opn4LacZ/DTA mice (Supplementary file 1), and consistent with our previous report, about 125 M1 ipRGCs survived in Opn4LacZ/aDTA mice (Güler et al., 2008) (Figure 1F; Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Güler et al., 2008 and data shown in Figure 1F

claims.claim: Some ipRGCs that express high levels of melanopsin (M1s) can survive the presence of a single dose of the full strength DTA.
claims.source: These results show that even some ipRGCs that express high levels of melanopsin (M1s) can survive the presence of a single dose of the full strength DTA.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that some M1 ipRGCs survive in DTA mice

claims.claim: Sparse retinal fibers were found in the SCN of heterozygous DTA mice (Opn4DTA/+).
claims.source: Sparse retinal fibers were found in the SCN of heterozygous DTA mice (Opn4DTA/+) as observed in Opn4Cre/DTA; Z/AP mice (Figure 1A) but these retinal fibers were entirely absent in Opn4DTA/DTA mice (Figure 1D) suggesting that Opn4DTA/DTA mice have more extensive ipRGC loss than Opn4DTA/+ mice.
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1A and 1D

claims.claim: Retinal fibers were entirely absent in the SCN of Opn4DTA/DTA mice.
claims.source: Sparse retinal fibers were found in the SCN of heterozygous DTA mice (Opn4DTA/+) as observed in Opn4Cre/DTA; Z/AP mice (Figure 1A) but these retinal fibers were entirely absent in Opn4DTA/DTA mice (Figure 1D) suggesting that Opn4DTA/DTA mice have more extensive ipRGC loss than Opn4DTA/+ mice.
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1D

claims.claim: Opn4DTA/DTA mice have more extensive ipRGC loss than Opn4DTA/+ mice.
claims.source: Sparse retinal fibers were found in the SCN of heterozygous DTA mice (Opn4DTA/+) as observed in Opn4Cre/DTA; Z/AP mice (Figure 1A) but these retinal fibers were entirely absent in Opn4DTA/DTA mice (Figure 1D) suggesting that Opn4DTA/DTA mice have more extensive ipRGC loss than Opn4DTA/+ mice.
claims.evidence: Inferred from comparison of SCN innervation patterns in Figure 1A and 1D

claims.claim: General retinal structure appeared similar between wild-type and Opn4DTA/DTA mice by hematoxylin and eosin staining and fluorescent staining for various retinal cell types.
claims.source: Wild-type and Opn4DTA/DTA mice appeared similar by these stains, and quantification of total retinal thickness, as well as the thickness of each of the retinal layers, based on hematoxylin and eosin staining showed no difference between wild-type and Opn4DTA/DTA mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,E–F and 1D

claims.claim: There was no difference in the number of SMI-32-positive ganglion cells, Brn3a-positive ganglion cells, cones, and starburst amacrine cells between wild-type and Opn4DTA/DTA mice.
claims.source: We also counted the number of SMI-32-positive ganglion cells, Brn3a-positive ganglion cells, cones, and starburst amacrine cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–J). When we compared wild-type and Opn4DTA/DTA mice, there was no difference in cell number of any of these cell types.
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–J

claims.claim: About 50% of SMI-32 positive ganglion cells are M4 ipRGCs.
claims.source: It is relevant to mention that about 50% of SMI-32 positive ganglion cells are actually M4 ipRGCs (Estevez et al., 2012; Schmidt et al., 2014), which express lower levels of melanopsin compared to M1 ipRGCs (Ecker et al., 2010; Sexton et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Estevez et al., 2012 and Schmidt et al., 2014

claims.claim: M4 ipRGCs express lower levels of melanopsin compared to M1 ipRGCs.
claims.source: It is relevant to mention that about 50% of SMI-32 positive ganglion cells are actually M4 ipRGCs (Estevez et al., 2012; Schmidt et al., 2014), which express lower levels of melanopsin compared to M1 ipRGCs (Ecker et al., 2010; Sexton et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Ecker et al., 2010 and Sexton et al., 2015

claims.claim: Expression of two copies of DTA from the melanopsin locus does not kill all ipRGCs.
claims.source: Thus, expression of two copies of DTA from the melanopsin locus does not even succeed in killing all ipRGCs.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that SMI-32 positive cells (including M4 ipRGCs) survive in Opn4DTA/DTA mice

claims.claim: There was no difference between wild-type and Opn4DTA/DTA mice in the number of nuclei or neurons in the SCN.
claims.source: To assess potential off target effects in relevant brain regions, we counted the total number of nuclei (based on DAPI staining) and the total number of neurons (identified by antibody staining for Hu) in the SCN of wild-type and Opn4DTA/DTA mice. There was no difference between wild-type and Opn4DTA/DTA mice in the number of nuclei or neurons when compared in total or section by section through the SCN (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claims.claim: The total size of the dLGN was not different between wild-type and Opn4DTA/DTA mice or among any other tested mouse lines.
claims.source: Furthermore, the total size of the dLGN was also not different between wild-type and Opn4DTA/DTA mice or among any other tested mouse lines (Figure 4—figure supplement 4E).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4E

claims.claim: DTA efficiently and selectively ablated ipRGCs at early postnatal ages.
claims.source: These data combined demonstrate that DTA efficiently and selectively ablated ipRGCs at early postnatal ages.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the combined data showing ipRGC loss without off-target effects

claims.claim: Opn4LacZ/LacZ and wild-type mice showed normal photoentrainment, phase shifting (at CT16), and free-running periods.
claims.source: Opn4LacZ/LacZ and wild-type mice showed normal photoentrainment, phase shifting (at CT16), and free-running periods (Figure 2A–C).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2A–C

claims.claim: Opn4aDTA/aDTA mice were unable to photoentrain or phase shift and free-ran under all lighting conditions with a period comparable to controls.
claims.source: As previously published, Opn4aDTA/aDTA mice were unable to photoentrain or phase shift and free-ran under all lighting conditions with a period comparable to controls (Güler et al., 2008) (Figure 2A–C).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Güler et al., 2008 and data shown in Figure 2A–C

claims.claim: Opn4DTA/+ mice photoentrained, phase shifted (at CT16), and free-ran in constant darkness with a normal circadian period.
claims.source: Opn4DTA/+ mice photoentrained, phase shifted (at CT16), and free-ran in constant darkness with a normal circadian period (Figure 2A–C) indicating that residual retinal input to the SCN in heterozygotes is sufficient for circadian photoentrainment.
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2A–C

claims.claim: Residual retinal input to the SCN in Opn4DTA/+ heterozygotes is sufficient for circadian photoentrainment.
claims.source: Opn4DTA/+ mice photoentrained, phase shifted (at CT16), and free-ran in constant darkness with a normal circadian period (Figure 2A–C) indicating that residual retinal input to the SCN in heterozygotes is sufficient for circadian photoentrainment.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that Opn4DTA/+ mice photoentrain normally despite partial ipRGC loss

claims.claim: In Opn4DTA/LacZ mice, circadian responses to light were highly attenuated, with inconsistent entrainment and phase-shifting, and exhibited a free-running period comparable to control mice.
claims.source: In these mice, circadian responses to light were highly attenuated, with inconsistent entrainment and phase-shifting, and exhibited a free-running period comparable to control mice (Figure 2A–C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2A–C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claims.claim: Opn4DTA/DTA mice did not photoentrain and free-ran with an abnormally lengthened period.
claims.source: Similar to Opn4aDTA/aDTA mice, Opn4DTA/DTA mice did not photoentrain; however, they free-ran with an abnormally lengthened period (Figure 2A,B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2A,B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B

claims.claim: Full-strength DTA, but not aDTA, kills ipRGCs during early development.
claims.source: Because full-strength DTA, but not aDTA, kills ipRGCs during early development, these findings suggested the hypothesis that ipRGCs act during early postnatal ages to establish a normal circadian period length.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the differential timing of ipRGC ablation between DTA and aDTA mice

claims.claim: ipRGCs act during early postnatal ages to establish a normal circadian period length.
claims.source: Because full-strength DTA, but not aDTA, kills ipRGCs during early development, these findings suggested the hypothesis that ipRGCs act during early postnatal ages to establish a normal circadian period length.
claims.evidence: Hypothesis inferred from the observation that early but not late ipRGC ablation causes lengthened period

claims.claim: Loss of ipRGC innervation does not drastically alter SCN development.
claims.source: We performed a general examination of expression of transcription factors important for SCN development and a neuropeptide relevant for clock function to examine the SCN, and found no apparent disruption in the SCN of Opn4DTA/DTA mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2). Thus, loss of ipRGC innervation does not drastically alter SCN development, and it is possible the lengthened period stems from a loss of direct ipRGC-dependent regulation of SCN neurons.
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claims.claim: The lengthened period in Opn4DTA/DTA mice may stem from a loss of direct ipRGC-dependent regulation of SCN neurons.
claims.source: Thus, loss of ipRGC innervation does not drastically alter SCN development, and it is possible the lengthened period stems from a loss of direct ipRGC-dependent regulation of SCN neurons.
claims.evidence: Speculative explanation for the lengthened period phenotype

claims.claim: The lengthened period effect in Opn4DTA/DTA mice could be due to altered input from the intergeniculate leaflet (IGL), which also receives innervation by ipRGCs.
claims.source: Alternatively, this effect could be due to altered input from the intergeniculate leaflet (IGL), which also receives innervation by ipRGCs.
claims.evidence: Alternative speculative explanation for the lengthened period phenotype

claims.claim: Mice enucleated at P0 exhibited a lengthened circadian period similar to Opn4DTA/DTA mice.
claims.source: However, mice enucleated at P0 exhibited a lengthened circadian period similar to Opn4DTA/DTA mice, whereas mice enucleated at P60 phenocopied Opn4aDTA/aDTA mice exhibiting a period comparable to intact mice (Figure 2A–B,D–E).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2D–E

claims.claim: Mice enucleated at P60 exhibited a period comparable to intact mice.
claims.source: However, mice enucleated at P0 exhibited a lengthened circadian period similar to Opn4DTA/DTA mice, whereas mice enucleated at P60 phenocopied Opn4aDTA/aDTA mice exhibiting a period comparable to intact mice (Figure 2A–B,D–E).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2D–E

claims.claim: Circadian period length has been shown to be stable in adult mice kept under constant darkness for 2 months.
claims.source: Circadian period length has been shown to be stable in adult mice kept under constant darkness for 2 months (Campuzano et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Campuzano et al., 1999

claims.claim: ipRGCs function postnatally to set the length of the circadian period.
claims.source: Thus, these data corroborate results from Opn4DTA/DTA mice indicating that ipRGCs function postnatally to set the length of the circadian period.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the enucleation experiments showing age-dependent effects on period length

claims.claim: Most (9 of 16) dark-reared mice exhibited a longer intrinsic circadian period than mice raised in a 12:12-LD cycle.
claims.source: While the phenotype was less penetrant than that the Opn4DTA/DTA mice and P0 enucleates, most (9 of 16) dark-reared mice exhibited a longer intrinsic circadian period than mice raised in a 12:12-LD cycle and this was stable for duration of our recordings (up to 60 days; Figure 3A,B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3A,B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claims.claim: The lengthened period of dark-reared animals was comparable to that exhibited by mice enucleated at P0 and mice with early postnatal ablation of ipRGCs (Opn4DTA/DTA).
claims.source: The lengthened period of the dark-reared animals was comparable to that exhibited by mice enucleated at P0 and mice with early postnatal ablation of ipRGCs (Opn4DTA/DTA) (Figures 2 and 3; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by comparison of data in Figures 2 and 3

claims.claim: Light contributes to the process of establishing circadian period length in mammals.
claims.source: It has been thought that the mammalian circadian period length was established independent of sensory input, but our data show that light contributes to this process.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the dark-rearing experiments showing light-dependent effects on period length

claims.claim: In zebrafish, light is required to initiate expression of clock genes and for generation of rhythms.
claims.source: In zebrafish, it is known that light is required to initiate expression of clock genes and for generation of rhythms (Ben-Moshe et al., 2014; Kazimi and Cahill, 1999; Ziv et al., 2005); however, this is the first evidence to indicate that light is also required for mammalian clock maturation.
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Ben-Moshe et al., 2014; Kazimi and Cahill, 1999; Ziv et al., 2005

claims.claim: This is the first evidence to indicate that light is required for mammalian clock maturation.
claims.source: In zebrafish, it is known that light is required to initiate expression of clock genes and for generation of rhythms (Ben-Moshe et al., 2014; Kazimi and Cahill, 1999; Ziv et al., 2005); however, this is the first evidence to indicate that light is also required for mammalian clock maturation.
claims.evidence: Claim about novelty of the finding based on the experimental results

claims.claim: Upon exposure to a 12:12-LD-cycle, dark-reared mice photoentrained, and light exposure during photoentrainment was sufficient to normalize the circadian period length.
claims.source: Upon exposure to a 12:12-LD-cycle, dark-reared mice photoentrained, and light exposure during photoentrainment was sufficient to normalize the circadian period length (Figure 3A,B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3A,B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claims.claim: A single short light pulse (3 hr), which did not cause photoentrainment, was sufficient to set the circadian period of dark-reared animals.
claims.source: Furthermore, a single short light pulse (3 hr), which did not cause photoentrainment, (Figure 3C,D) was also sufficient to set the circadian period of dark-reared animals (Figure 3C,D).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3C,D

claims.claim: Brief light exposure is sufficient to set the circadian period and can occur in adults.
claims.source: These data indicate that brief light exposure is sufficient to set the circadian period and can even occur in adults, thus, indicating a lack of a critical developmental window for this process.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the light pulse experiments showing period normalization in adult dark-reared mice

claims.claim: There is no critical developmental window for light to set the circadian period.
claims.source: These data indicate that brief light exposure is sufficient to set the circadian period and can even occur in adults, thus, indicating a lack of a critical developmental window for this process.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that adult light exposure can normalize period in dark-reared mice

claims.claim: By P7, ipRGCs have reached their central targets in the brain.
claims.source: By P7, ipRGCs have reached their central targets in the brain (Figure 1A–B) (McNeill et al., 2011) and a subset of ipRGCs forms intra-retinal collateral axons that terminate in the inner plexiform layer, where they synapse onto dopaminergic amacrine cells (Joo et al., 2013; Prigge et al., 2016) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to McNeill et al., 2011 and data shown in Figure 1A–B

claims.claim: A subset of ipRGCs forms intra-retinal collateral axons that terminate in the inner plexiform layer, where they synapse onto dopaminergic amacrine cells.
claims.source: By P7, ipRGCs have reached their central targets in the brain (Figure 1A–B) (McNeill et al., 2011) and a subset of ipRGCs forms intra-retinal collateral axons that terminate in the inner plexiform layer, where they synapse onto dopaminergic amacrine cells (Joo et al., 2013; Prigge et al., 2016) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Joo et al., 2013 and Prigge et al., 2016, and data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claims.claim: P7 is in the middle of a critical developmental period for the image-forming visual system.
claims.source: P7 is in the middle of a critical developmental period for the image-forming visual system.
claims.evidence: Based on established knowledge about visual system development

claims.claim: From P0-P14, the retinotopic map is being refined by spontaneously generated neural activity in the retina, termed retinal waves.
claims.source: From P0-P14, the retinotopic map is being refined by spontaneously generated neural activity in the retina, termed retinal waves (Ackman et al., 2012; Feller, 2009; Feller et al., 1996; McLaughlin et al., 2003; Meister et al., 1991; Ramoa et al., 1989; Shatz, 1990; Stellwagen and Shatz, 2002; Xu et al. 2011; Zhang et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work on retinal waves

claims.claim: The presence of intra-retinal collaterals on ipRGCs at early postnatal ages provides anatomical means for ipRGCs to influence the retina during an important developmental window.
claims.source: The presence of intra-retinal collaterals on ipRGCs at early postnatal ages provides anatomical means for ipRGCs to influence the retina during an important developmental window.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the anatomical observation of intra-retinal collaterals and the timing of visual system development

claims.claim: While retinal innervation of the superior colliculus in Opn4DTA/DTA mice was comparable to wild-type, eye-specific axonal segregation in the dLGN was severely disrupted.
claims.source: To investigate this, we traced the axonal projections of retinal ganglion cells in adult wild-type and Opn4DTA/DTA mice, and observed that, while retinal innervation of the superior colliculus in Opn4DTA/DTA mice was comparable to wild-type (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), eye-specific axonal segregation in the dLGN was severely disrupted (Figure 4A,B; Figure 4—figure supplements 3 and 4).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and Figure 4A,B

claims.claim: In Opn4DTA/DTA mice, the ipsilateral zone in the dLGN had poorly defined boundaries and substantial contralateral innervation.
claims.source: In Opn4DTA/DTA mice, the ipsilateral zone had poorly defined boundaries and substantial contralateral innervation (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4A

claims.claim: In Opn4DTA/DTA mice, there was a significant increase in the percentage of pixels with overlapping input from the two eyes in the dLGN.
claims.source: In Opn4DTA/DTA mice, there was a significant increase in the percentage of pixels with overlapping input from the two eyes, and this eye-specific segregation defect was most severe in the caudal dLGN (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 4F).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 4F

claims.claim: The eye-specific segregation defect in Opn4DTA/DTA mice was most severe in the caudal dLGN.
claims.source: In Opn4DTA/DTA mice, there was a significant increase in the percentage of pixels with overlapping input from the two eyes, and this eye-specific segregation defect was most severe in the caudal dLGN (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 4F).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 4F

claims.claim: The total amount of ipsilateral and contralateral input and total dLGN size were similar across all tested genotypes.
claims.source: The total amount of ipsilateral and contralateral input and total dLGN size were similar across all tested genotypes (Figure 4C,D, Figure 4—figure supplement 4C–E).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4C,D and Figure 4—figure supplement 4C–E

claims.claim: Abnormal eye-specific segregation was not observed in either melanopsin knockout mice (Opn4LacZ/LacZ) or mice with ipRGCs ablated during adulthood (Opn4aDTA/aDTA).
claims.source: Abnormal eye-specific segregation was not observed in either melanopsin knockout mice (Opn4LacZ/LacZ) or mice with ipRGCs ablated during adulthood (Opn4aDTA/aDTA) (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A–D).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4A–D

claims.claim: Opn4DTA/+ mice exhibited disrupted eye-specific segregation that was intermediate between wild-type and Opn4DTA/DTA mice.
claims.source: Importantly, Opn4DTA/+ mice, which have substantial ipRGC loss, although to lesser degree than Opn4DTA/DTA mice, exhibited disrupted eye-specific segregation that was intermediate between wild-type and Opn4DTA/DTA mice (Figure 4A,B, Figure 4—figure supplement 4F).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4A,B and Figure 4—figure supplement 4F

claims.claim: ipRGCs have a developmental role in the segregation of all RGC inputs to the dLGN.
claims.source: Combined, these data reveal an developmental role for ipRGCs in the segregation of all RGC inputs to the dLGN.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that ipRGC ablation disrupts eye-specific segregation

claims.claim: Eye-specific segregation deficits in Opn4DTA/DTA mice were observed by P8.
claims.source: To conclusively determine whether ipRGCs function during early postnatal ages to regulate refinement of retinogeniculate projections, we examined eye-specific segregation at P8 and, similar to adult mice, found an increase in overlapping ipsilateral and contralateral projections in Opn4DTA/DTA mice, but no difference in total retinal input compared to wild-type (Figure 5A–D).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5A–D

claims.claim: ipRGCs function at early postnatal ages to mediate refinement of the image-forming visual system by regulating eye-specific segregation of retinogeniculate projections.
claims.source: These data indicate that ipRGCs function at early postnatal ages to mediate refinement of the image-forming visual system by regulating eye-specific segregation of retinogeniculate projections.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation of segregation deficits at P8 in Opn4DTA/DTA mice

claims.claim: Opn4DTA/DTA animals exhibited reduced visual acuity compared to controls (wild-type and Opn4LacZ/LacZ) by both the virtual optomotor system and the visual water task.
claims.source: To examine the functional consequence of altered eye-specific segregation, we compared wild-type, Opn4LacZ/LacZ, and Opn4DTA/DTA mice in two behavioral tests of visual acuity: the virtual optomotor system and the visual water task (Douglas et al., 2005; Prusky et al., 2000). By both measures, Opn4DTA/DTA animals exhibited reduced visual acuity compared to controls (wild-type and Opn4LacZ/LacZ; Figure 4E,F).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4E,F

claims.claim: Opn4DTA/+ mice exhibited an intermediate reduction in visual acuity compared to wild-type and Opn4DTA/DTA mice.
claims.source: Remarkably, Opn4DTA/+ mice also exhibited an intermediate reduction in visual acuity (Figure 4E,F).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4E,F

claims.claim: The severity of the deficits in eye-specific segregation and visual functions were correlated with the extent of ipRGC loss.
claims.source: Thus, the severity of the deficits in eye-specific segregation and visual functions were correlated with the extent of ipRGC loss.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the comparison of phenotypes across genotypes with different degrees of ipRGC loss

claims.claim: Spiking properties of RGCs during waves were significantly altered in Opn4DTA/DTA mice.
claims.source: Spiking properties of RGCs during waves were significantly altered in Opn4DTA/DTA mice. Wave-associated bursts (WABs) were significantly longer in duration, and had higher firing rates, and shorter inter-burst intervals (Figure 5E,G–H, Supplementary file 2) than they did in wild-type controls.
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5E,G–H and Supplementary file 2

claims.claim: Wave-associated bursts (WABs) were significantly longer in duration in Opn4DTA/DTA mice compared to wild-type controls.
claims.source: Wave-associated bursts (WABs) were significantly longer in duration, and had higher firing rates, and shorter inter-burst intervals (Figure 5E,G–H, Supplementary file 2) than they did in wild-type controls.
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5E,G–H and Supplementary file 2

claims.claim: WABs had higher firing rates in Opn4DTA/DTA mice compared to wild-type controls.
claims.source: Wave-associated bursts (WABs) were significantly longer in duration, and had higher firing rates, and shorter inter-burst intervals (Figure 5E,G–H, Supplementary file 2) than they did in wild-type controls.
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5E,G–H and Supplementary file 2

claims.claim: WABs had shorter inter-burst intervals in Opn4DTA/DTA mice compared to wild-type controls.
claims.source: Wave-associated bursts (WABs) were significantly longer in duration, and had higher firing rates, and shorter inter-burst intervals (Figure 5E,G–H, Supplementary file 2) than they did in wild-type controls.
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5E,G–H and Supplementary file 2

claims.claim: There were significantly more total spikes as well as more spikes outside of bursts in Opn4DTA/DTA mice compared to wild-type controls.
claims.source: There were also significantly more total spikes as well as more spikes outside of bursts (Figure 5E,G–H, Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5E,G–H and Supplementary file 2

claims.claim: Correlated spiking activity between neurons was very similar between wild-type and Opn4DTA/DTA genotypes.
claims.source: Correlated spiking activity between neurons was very similar between the genotypes, as measured by the spike time tiling coefficient (STTC; [Cutts and Eglen, 2014])(Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5F

claims.claim: ipRGCs are critical for normal retinal wave activity, even in darkness.
claims.source: These data indicate that ipRGCs are critical for normal retinal wave activity, even in darkness, and together with our anatomical findings (Figure 4A–D; Figure 4—figure supplements 3–4), allow us to suggest that ipRGCs mediate eye-specific segregation of RGC projections to the dLGN by regulating the spiking properties of conventional RGCs during retinal waves.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the altered retinal wave properties in Opn4DTA/DTA mice

claims.claim: ipRGCs mediate eye-specific segregation of RGC projections to the dLGN by regulating the spiking properties of conventional RGCs during retinal waves.
claims.source: These data indicate that ipRGCs are critical for normal retinal wave activity, even in darkness, and together with our anatomical findings (Figure 4A–D; Figure 4—figure supplements 3–4), allow us to suggest that ipRGCs mediate eye-specific segregation of RGC projections to the dLGN by regulating the spiking properties of conventional RGCs during retinal waves.
claims.evidence: Suggested mechanism based on combined anatomical and electrophysiological findings

claims.claim: There are currently five identified subtypes of ipRGCs.
claims.source: There are currently five identified subtypes of ipRGCs.
claims.evidence: Based on established knowledge in the field

claims.claim: M1 ipRGCs project to non-image-forming brain centers, while M2-M5 ipRGCs project at least in part to image-forming targets.
claims.source: M1 ipRGCs project to non-image-forming brain centers, while M2-M5 ipRGCs project at least in part to image-forming targets (Ecker et al., 2010; Schmidt et al., 2011; Schmidt and Kofuji, 2009).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Ecker et al., 2010; Schmidt et al., 2011; Schmidt and Kofuji, 2009

claims.claim: The M1 subtype can be further subdivided based on expression of the transcription factor Pou4f2 (also referred to as Brn3b), which is also expressed in all non-M1 ipRGCs.
claims.source: The M1 subtype can be further subdivided based on expression of the transcription factor Pou4f2 (also referred to as Brn3b), which is also expressed in all non-M1 ipRGCs (Chen et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2011

results.result: The authors generated a new mouse line (Opn4DTA) expressing full-strength diphtheria toxin from the melanopsin locus, which causes early postnatal ablation of ipRGCs. This ablation is more extensive than the previously published attenuated DTA line (Opn4aDTA), which ablates ipRGCs only in adulthood. The DTA efficiently and selectively ablates ipRGCs without off-target effects on other retinal cell types or brain regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C18 provide comprehensive characterization of the DTA mouse line through multiple complementary approaches including cell counts at different developmental stages (C3-C6), anatomical assessment of SCN innervation (C8-C10), histological analysis of retinal structure (C11-C12), and quantification of off-target effects (C16-C17). The data consistently demonstrate selective ipRGC ablation beginning at early postnatal ages with the full-strength DTA, contrasting with adult-onset ablation in aDTA mice.

results.result: Early postnatal ablation of ipRGCs in Opn4DTA/DTA mice results in a lengthened circadian free-running period, while adult ablation in Opn4aDTA/aDTA mice does not affect period length. This suggests that ipRGCs function during early postnatal development to establish normal circadian period length, though the mechanism remains unclear.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C24 provide wheel-running behavioral data across multiple genotypes showing that only early ipRGC ablation (Opn4DTA/DTA) causes lengthened period, while adult ablation (Opn4aDTA/aDTA) and partial ablation (Opn4DTA/+) do not. Claims C25-C26 appropriately infer the developmental timing requirement. However, C27-C29 acknowledge uncertainty about mechanism, with C28-C29 being speculative. The core finding is well-supported by the data.

results.result: Enucleation experiments confirm that removal of retinal input at P0, but not P60, causes a lengthened circadian period similar to Opn4DTA/DTA mice, corroborating that ipRGCs function postnatally to set circadian period length.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C31 present enucleation data showing age-dependent effects on period length that phenocopy the genetic ablation results. C32 provides supporting literature context. C33 appropriately synthesizes these findings. The enucleation approach provides independent validation of the developmental timing requirement identified in the genetic ablation experiments.

results.result: Dark-rearing experiments reveal that light exposure during postnatal development is required to establish normal circadian period length in mammals. Most dark-reared mice exhibited lengthened periods comparable to P0 enucleates and Opn4DTA/DTA mice, representing the first evidence that light is required for mammalian clock maturation.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C35 present dark-rearing data showing that 9 of 16 mice exhibited lengthened periods comparable to early ipRGC ablation. C36 appropriately infers light's role. C37 provides comparative context from zebrafish. C38 claims novelty for mammals. While the phenotype is less penetrant than genetic ablation (56% vs nearly 100%), the authors acknowledge this and provide a reasonable explanation. The finding is novel and well-supported despite incomplete penetrance.

results.result: Light exposure can normalize the circadian period of dark-reared mice even in adulthood. A single 3-hour light pulse is sufficient to set the period, indicating there is no critical developmental window for this light-dependent process.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C40 present data showing that both prolonged light exposure during photoentrainment and a brief 3-hour light pulse can normalize period in dark-reared adults. C41-C42 appropriately infer the lack of a critical window. This is a striking finding that distinguishes this process from many other developmental phenomena and is well-supported by the experimental data.

results.result: By P7, ipRGCs have reached their central brain targets and a subset forms intra-retinal collateral axons that synapse onto dopaminergic amacrine cells. This timing coincides with the critical period for retinal wave-dependent refinement of the image-forming visual system (P0-P14), providing anatomical means for ipRGCs to influence retinal development.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C44 are supported by citations and anatomical data showing ipRGC projections and intra-retinal collaterals by P7. C45-C46 provide established developmental context. C47 appropriately infers the anatomical basis for ipRGC influence during this critical period. This sets up the rationale for investigating ipRGC roles in visual system development.

results.result: Early postnatal ablation of ipRGCs in Opn4DTA/DTA mice severely disrupts eye-specific segregation in the dLGN, with poorly defined ipsilateral zone boundaries and increased overlap between contralateral and ipsilateral projections. This defect is not observed in melanopsin knockout mice or mice with adult ipRGC ablation, and shows a dose-dependent relationship with the extent of ipRGC loss.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C52 present comprehensive anatomical data using CTB tracing and two independent quantification methods showing disrupted segregation in Opn4DTA/DTA mice. C53 demonstrates specificity by showing normal segregation in control genotypes. C54 shows dose-dependence in heterozygotes. C55 appropriately synthesizes these findings. The convergent evidence from multiple approaches strongly supports a developmental role for ipRGCs in eye-specific segregation.

results.result: Eye-specific segregation deficits are already present at P8 in Opn4DTA/DTA mice, confirming that ipRGCs function during early postnatal ages to regulate refinement of retinogeniculate projections.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C57 present P8 anatomical data showing segregation deficits are already established early in development, directly demonstrating the developmental timing of ipRGC function. This is critical evidence that the adult phenotype reflects a developmental defect rather than ongoing ipRGC function.

results.result: Opn4DTA/DTA mice exhibit reduced visual acuity in two independent behavioral assays (virtual optomotor system and visual water task), with Opn4DTA/+ mice showing intermediate deficits. The severity of visual deficits correlates with the extent of ipRGC loss.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C59 present behavioral data from two independent visual acuity tests showing dose-dependent deficits. C60 appropriately infers the correlation. The use of two different behavioral paradigms strengthens the conclusion. The dose-dependent effect in heterozygotes provides additional support for a causal relationship between ipRGC loss and visual deficits.

results.result: Retinal wave properties are significantly altered in P6 Opn4DTA/DTA mice recorded in darkness, with longer wave-associated bursts, higher firing rates, shorter inter-burst intervals, and more spikes outside bursts, while correlated activity between neurons remains normal. This indicates ipRGCs regulate retinal wave activity independent of light and suggests they mediate eye-specific segregation by regulating RGC spiking properties during waves.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C66 present detailed multielectrode array recordings showing specific alterations in retinal wave properties in darkness. The data are comprehensive and statistically analyzed. C67 appropriately infers ipRGC regulation of waves independent of light. C68 proposes a mechanistic link to segregation deficits, which is reasonable given the combined anatomical and electrophysiological findings, though the authors appropriately use cautious language ('suggest').

results.result: A small population of approximately 200 Pou4f2-negative M1 ipRGCs that project exclusively to circadian centers and form intra-retinal collaterals is sufficient for both setting the circadian period and proper eye-specific segregation of retinogeniculate projections, as demonstrated by normal phenotypes in Opn4Cre/+; Pou4f2Z-DTA/+ mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C76 provide background on ipRGC subtypes and characterization of the Opn4Cre/+; Pou4f2Z-DTA/+ mouse line, supported by citations and anatomical data. C77-C79 present behavioral and anatomical data showing normal circadian period and eye-specific segregation in these mice. C80-C81 appropriately synthesize these findings to identify the critical ipRGC subpopulation. This is a key result that narrows down which ipRGCs are necessary and sufficient for both developmental processes.

results.result: Light plays an essential role in setting the circadian period but not in the image-forming visual process of eye-specific segregation, as demonstrated by dark-rearing experiments affecting period but not segregation deficits in Opn4DTA/DTA mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C83 synthesize findings from dark-rearing experiments (showing light-dependent period setting) and the observation that segregation deficits occur in Opn4DTA/DTA mice regardless of light exposure. This differential light requirement distinguishes the two developmental processes and is well-supported by the combined experimental evidence.

results.result: A subset of approximately 200 Pou4f2-negative M1 ipRGCs constitute a shared node in neural circuits mediating light-dependent maturation of the circadian clock and light-independent refinement of retinogeniculate projections, revealing unexpected crosstalk between historically distinct image-forming and non-image-forming visual systems.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C91 synthesize the major findings of the study. C85-C86 provide context about the traditional separation of visual subsystems. C87-C90 summarize the key experimental findings. C91 appropriately integrates these to present the overarching conclusion. This synthesis is well-supported by the comprehensive experimental evidence presented throughout the manuscript.
